components.text: The exclusion of closed causal loops needs a defended transitivity principle, not mere stipulation.
The exclusion of closed causal loops requires a defended transitivity principle rather than mere stipulation.
Loop-permitting theories require separate treatment of dynamic and static causal loops.
Dynamic loops are said to inherit the independently argued problem of infinite regress.
Static loops are said to involve vicious self-dependence rather than merely disputed transitivity.
Loop-permitting accounts need an answer to the alleged regress or circular dependence generated by dynamic and static loops.
The stated premises yield at least one first cause, not exactly one uniquely existing first cause.
The stated causal premises establish existential first causes but supply no premise establishing exactly one first cause.
A causeless initial universe allegedly lacks any prior differentiator restricting causeless beginning to that universe.
The claimed metaphysical necessity of the initial state must block the predicted proliferation of uncaused alternatives.
A uniquely causeless initial universe needs a principled restriction preventing other universes or events from beginning causelessly.
The theory itself restricts natural reality to the necessary initial state and its causal evolution.
The absence of a cause selecting the initial state allegedly permits causeless later entities to appear.
The necessary-initial-state theory itself restricts membership in natural reality to the initial state and its causal evolution.
The actual initial universe needs a differentiating basis relative to other logically describable universes.
A theory-level restriction allegedly prevents other causeless possibilities from becoming actual.
The claim of a uniquely actual necessary initial state must distinguish that state from other consistently describable universes.
A natural initial state can begin without a prior temporal regress if it is metaphysically necessary.
The naturalist account restricts later reality through causal evolution rather than timeless changeless existence.
A beginningless first cause can avoid temporal regress if it is timeless and initially changeless rather than temporally extended.
Changelessness allegedly requires a duration whose measure must be finite or infinite.
If the duration is infinite there is a regress; if finite, the changeless condition has a beginning.
The proposed changeless condition allegedly requires a duration whose measure is either finite or infinite.
Adding a personal God must provide explanatory work beyond that done by an initial foundation and causal evolution.
The proposed transcendent and immaterial cause adds an entity beyond the initial universe.
The timeless cause is treated as an additional theoretical posit rather than an explanatory necessity.
Adding a personal divine cause must provide explanatory benefit beyond a universe-internal necessary initial stage.
A theory cannot restrict causeless beginning merely by asserting that only its initial item is uncaused.
Intrinsic differences arise only after existence and therefore cannot explain a uniquely permitted uncaused beginning.
Surrounding circumstances are compatible with other beginnings and do not provide the restriction.
The proposed restriction on causeless beginnings cannot be grounded in a cause, later intrinsic differences, or compatible circumstances.
Logical consistency of alternative universes does not establish their metaphysical possibility or eligibility for actuality.
The proliferation argument ranges over alternatives without establishing that they are metaphysically possible under the rival theory.
The pro argument treats logical consistency as sufficient evidence that alternative universes are metaphysically possible.
The relevant claim concerns inability to cease or fail in an initial state, not existence in every logically possible world.
Possible-world necessity is not the modal burden the pro says its beginningless first cause must satisfy.
The pro necessity claim is narrower than existence in every logically possible world and concerns an unsustained first cause's initial state.
An event occurring wholly at the initial instant may lack a distinct beginning, defeating the universal event-begins premise.
The initial-state modal clarification does not establish that an instantaneous initial event has a separate beginning.
An event wholly occurring at the first instant may not possess a distinct temporal beginning within that instant.
A first cause need not be outside the universe because the rival assumptions yield a universe-internal first cause.
Establishing some first cause does not by itself select a personal creator over a universe-internal foundation.
Different modal assumptions can locate the first cause within the universe rather than outside it.
A first-cause conclusion does not by itself prefer a personal external cause over a universe-internal initial cause.
